item.title: I-T dept nudges UAE property owners as FAST-DS gets 1,100 declarations
item.description: The Income Tax Department is stepping up outreach to UAE property owners and other taxpayers as around 1,100 declarations have been filed under FAST-DS ahead of the December 31 deadline.
item.dc:creator: Monika Yadav
item.content:encoded: Around 1,100 taxpayers have filed declarations under the Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers – Disclosure Scheme, 2026 (FAST-DS), as the Income Tax Department steps up efforts to encourage disclosures before the December 31 deadline, sources in the Finance Ministry said. Announced in the Union Budget 2026-27, the scheme came into effect on August 16, 2026, offering eligible taxpayers a one-time opportunity to disclose specified foreign assets and income that were either not reported in tax returns or had not been offered to tax, subject to prescribed conditions. The department has begun selectively reaching out to taxpayers who own residential or commercial properties in the UAE that may not have been disclosed to the tax authorities, urging them to use the one-time window to regularise eligible holdings, sources said. Following a high-level meeting on October 23, the department has also decided to share additional information on foreign assets with relevant taxpayers wherever possible to help them identify holdings that may need to be disclosed under the scheme. The department is planning outreach programmes involving companies, educational institutions, professional bodies and industry associations to raise awareness about FAST-DS. The Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) has also set up committees in each region under the Principal Chief Commissioner of Income Tax to address taxpayers’ queries and concerns, sources added. The department has enabled a facility on its e-filing portal through which taxpayers can view and download information on foreign assets reported against their Permanent Account Numbers (PANs) by overseas jurisdictions under the Automatic Exchange of Information (AEOI) framework, including the Common Reporting Standard (CRS) and the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA). Information for calendar years 2022, 2023 and 2024 is currently available on the portal. The facility displays only information received from jurisdictions that are signatories to the CRS/FATCA frameworks. Information obtained under other multilateral arrangements has not been displayed because of risk factors or non-disclosure commitments. The department also gathers information and intelligence from other sources. At the October 23 meeting, it decided that such additional information could be shared with relevant taxpayers wherever possible, according to sources. Under one category of the scheme, eligible taxpayers can declare specified undisclosed foreign assets or income with an aggregate value of up to ₹1 crore by paying tax at 30 per cent of the fair market value as on March 31, 2026, along with an equal amount as a penalty, taking the combined levy to 60 per cent. A separate category covers eligible foreign assets acquired from income that has already been taxed or during a period when the taxpayer was a non-resident, but which were not subsequently reported in Schedule FA of the income-tax return. This category covers assets with an aggregate value of up to ₹5 crore and requires payment of a flat fee of ₹1 lakh, subject to the scheme’s conditions. A valid declaration and payment under the applicable category provide immunity from further assessment, penalty and prosecution under the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015. The scheme also allows taxpayers to report eligible accounted foreign assets for a fee of ₹1 lakh to avoid the annual non-reporting penalty of ₹10 lakh prescribed under the Black Money Act. “The restrictive monetary limits under FAST-DS may prevent a significant number of taxpayers from regularising their undisclosed foreign assets. Taxpayers with inherited foreign assets, in particular, may find it difficult to comply with the scheme because of the high tax and penalty burden on the current fair market value of assets, despite having limited liquidity to pay the amount,” said Sandeep Bhalla, partner at Dhruva Advisors. Bhalla suggested widening the scheme's eligibility criteria and removing value caps for inherited assets to encourage voluntary compliance and improve tax collections. Bhalla also called for extending the scheme’s deadline to March 31, 2027, and providing immunity to taxpayers declaring inherited foreign properties to encourage voluntary compliance.

item.title: Australia to tighten visa character checks from October 31: What changes
item.description: The revised rules will give greater weight to community safety and domestic violence concerns, while reducing the importance of family, employment and community ties in Australia ...
item.dc:creator: Amit Kumar
item.content:encoded: Australia will introduce stricter guidelines for refusing or cancelling visas on character grounds from October 31, 2026. It will make it harder for some visa holders to rely on their family, employment and community ties to argue against losing their right to stay in the country. Ministerial Direction 123, signed by Australian Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke on September 18, will replace the existing Direction 110. The revised framework changes how immigration officials assess character-related concerns, placing greater emphasis on protecting the Australian community from criminal activity, domestic and family violence, and other serious conduct. The changes will be relevant to Indian students, skilled workers, permanent residents and other visa holders who have a criminal history or whose conduct raises character concerns. What changes from October 31? The new direction reduces the number of primary considerations used in character-related visa decisions from five to four. These are community protection, domestic and family violence, the expectations of the Australian community, and the best interests of minor children in Australia. The most significant change concerns a person's ties to Australia. Previously treated as a primary consideration, factors such as length of residence, family relationships, employment and community contributions will move into the category of secondary considerations. This means that having lived in Australia for many years or having family members in the country may carry less weight when officials assess concerns about a person's character. The revised guidance also lowers the threshold for assessing certain future risks, using the possibility that a person might engage in particular conduct rather than requiring the decision-maker to conclude that the person would do so. Greater scrutiny of violence and other conduct The new framework expands the guidance on domestic and family violence, including how officials consider the conduct involved and its impact on victims and children. It also provides additional guidance on hate-related conduct, extremism, associations with prohibited groups and other behaviour that could raise concerns about a person's character. These changes are intended to influence how immigration officials weigh potential risks when deciding whether a person should be allowed to enter or remain in Australia. However, the underlying character test under Section 501 of Australia's Migration Act 1958 is not changing. Instead, Direction 123 changes how officials balance the relevant considerations after a person's circumstances raise a character-related issue. Who could be affected? The changes are particularly relevant to visa applicants and existing visa holders with criminal convictions, family violence matters or other adverse information that could affect their character assessment. Indian nationals with such histories should understand that strong family or professional connections in Australia may not carry the same weight as before. For example, a long-term resident with employment and family responsibilities in Australia could find it harder to rely on those circumstances if officials consider the person's conduct to pose a risk to the community. However, the revised direction does not mean that every person with a criminal record or an adverse history will automatically have their visa refused or cancelled. Decisions will depend on the circumstances of each case and the applicable legal requirements. Will pending applications also be affected? Direction 123 will apply to relevant decisions made on or after October 31, 2026, irrespective of when the visa application was lodged or when a cancellation review began. Consequently, people with pending character-related cases should not assume that the earlier guidance will apply simply because their applications or reviews started before the new rules take effect. What should Indian visa holders do? People concerned about their immigration status should review their circumstances before the new direction takes effect. Those facing character-related questions, including people with criminal convictions or family violence matters, should seek advice from a qualified Australian immigration professional. They should also ensure that information provided to immigration authorities is accurate and that relevant legal documents are available. The practical implication is that, from October 31, community protection will carry greater weight in character-related visa decisions. And, family, employment and other personal connections will generally be treated as secondary factors.

item.title: Hyundai targets 250,000 mid-size SUV sales in 2027 on Creta, Bayon push
item.description: MD and CEO Tarun Garg said the target is a baseline rather than a ceiling, as Hyundai expects the Creta and Bayon to appeal to different sets of mid-size SUV buyers ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Industry / Auto / Hyundai targets 250,000 mid-size SUV sales in 2027 on Creta, Bayon push

Hyundai targets 250,000 mid-size SUV sales in 2027 on Creta, Bayon push MD and CEO Tarun Garg said the target is a baseline rather than a ceiling, as Hyundai expects the Creta and Bayon to appeal to different sets of mid-size SUV buyers

Hyundai plans to begin exporting the Bayon two to six months after its domestic launch, following its usual product-export strategy (Photo: Reuters)

Deepak Patel 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 26 2026 | 3:50 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Hyundai Motor India Ltd (HMIL) is expecting sales of at least 250,000 units of mid-size sport utility vehicles (SUVs) -- which include Creta and newly launched Bayon -- in 2027 due to rapid growth being observed in the segment for past several years and the two models’ ability to attract different sets of buyers, its Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Tarun Garg said on Monday.   While speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the launch of the Bayon in Gurugram, Garg said the aforementioned target was a baseline rather than a ceiling. Bayon's deliveries are expected to begin during the ongoing festival season.     Garg said HMIL expects to sell around 170,000 units of the Creta in 2026. “The mid-SUV segment today is 16.5 per cent of the market already," he noted. The mid-size SUV segment in India has grown at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 25.6 per cent over the past five years and is projected to record 64 per cent volume growth between calendar years 2026 and 2032.   He said the segment’s size and growth made room for more than one model from the same manufacturer. Hyundai is now looking to build on the Creta’s established customer base through the Bayon.   The Bayon is being positioned differently from the Creta, with Hyundai targeting customers who are quicker to adopt new technology. Garg added that the distinction was based on customers’ attitudes and preferences rather than age, with the Creta drawing on its established brand value and loyal customer base, while the Bayon is aimed at buyers seeking a more technology-led experience. “Creta created a market (of mid-SUV segment) when it was launched 10 years. We expect that the launch of Bayon will allow us to do for next 10 years what Creta did then,” he stated.   Garg said Hyundai’s market research suggested petrol would account for the largest share of demand in the Bayon’s segment. The model will also get a compressed natural gas (CNG) option in January 2027. The company has not opted for a diesel version, as offering too many powertrain choices could complicate the product range and confuse buyers, he explained.   He also said user data generated through the Bayon’s artificial intelligence (AI)-powered voice assistant would remain with Hyundai and would not be shared with Perplexity, whose technology powers the underlying language model. SoundHound AI provides the voice technology and works with Hyundai globally.   Garg said Hyundai follows data privacy and security standards used in the United States and South Korea, where regulations are more developed than in India. “While some of these laws have not come to India, but they have been there in the US and Korea, much, much stronger," he stated.   Garg said Hyundai would continue selling the Verna despite the shrinking sedan market, as exports make the model viable. Verna was the company’s largest exported car, with domestic sales of around 7,000–10,000 units annually rising to 40,000–50,000 units when exports were included, he added.   “Verna has a very very important role in our portfolio. And we intend to continue with it even though the segment is de-growing,” he noted.   Hyundai plans to begin exporting the Bayon two to six months after its domestic launch, following its usual product-export strategy. Garg said the company would announce export destinations in due course. The SUV will be manufactured at Hyundai’s Chennai plant and is intended for more than 50 markets globally.   Garg also clarified that Hyundai Motor India’s $5 billion investment plan for 2025–2030 and Hyundai Motor Group’s $15.5 billion commitment for 2026–2032 have overlapping periods. He said spending planned for 2025 would be adjusted against the group’s broader plan, with additional investment expected to flow into the Indian subsidiary.   The company expects automatic transmissions to account for around 25 per cent of Bayon sales, with a margin of two percentage points either way. Garg said automatic transmission penetration across Hyundai’s portfolio was around 24-26 per cent, with the share generally higher in larger models.
